stem: A client with preeclampsia has new AST and ALT elevations to more than twice the upper limit of normal, and another hepatic diagnosis has been excluded. How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: It is evidence of impaired liver function that meets a severe-feature criterion for preeclampsia.
options.B: It establishes HELLP syndrome even if hemolysis and thrombocytopenia are absent.
options.C: It is an expected physiologic change of late pregnancy and does not indicate end-organ involvement.
options.D: It specifically demonstrates renal insufficiency rather than hepatic involvement.

rationale: A is correct. ACOG lists impaired liver function not explained by an alternative diagnosis, reflected by liver enzymes elevated to more than twice the upper limit of normal, as a severe feature of preeclampsia. B is incorrect because HELLP syndrome requires a broader syndrome of hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets; an isolated qualifying transaminase elevation does not by itself establish HELLP. C is incorrect because this degree of new transaminase elevation is not treated as a normal pregnancy change in the preeclampsia assessment. D is incorrect because AST and ALT are being used here to identify hepatic, not renal, end-organ involvement.
educational_objective: Interpret a new liver-transaminase elevation to more than twice the upper limit of normal, when not explained by another diagnosis, as impaired hepatic function and a severe feature of preeclampsia rather than as normal pregnancy physiology or HELLP syndrome by itself.
source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
source_document_title: Countdown to Intern Year, Week 3: Hypertensive Disorders; Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy
source_version_date: Current ACOG web guidance accessed 2026-08-17; severe-feature criteria reflect Practice Bulletin No. 222 framework
source_locator: Countdown to Intern Year, Week 3 — 'Preeclampsia with Severe Features': impaired liver function not accounted for by alternative diagnoses, indicated by liver enzymes more than twice the upper limit of normal, or severe persistent right-upper-quadrant/epigastric pain unresponsive to medication. Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy FAQ — 'How does preeclampsia affect the body?': severe features include abnormal kidney or liver function; HELLP is separately defined by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count.
source_claim_supported: In preeclampsia, liver transaminases elevated to more than twice the upper limit of normal without another hepatic explanation constitute impaired liver function and a severe feature; this finding alone does not establish HELLP syndrome.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor laboratory values and recognize trends or changes that can indicate potential complications; Appendix A includes prenatal complications and diagnostic/laboratory monitoring relevant to maternal hypertensive disorders.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — laboratory recognition of severe preeclampsia and hepatic end-organ involvement
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item into a precise laboratory-interpretation question using the official ACOG severe-feature threshold and the required qualifier that alternative hepatic diagnoses be excluded. Replaced obviously false distractors with clinically plausible confusion between severe preeclampsia, HELLP, normal pregnancy physiology, and renal involvement.

audit_findings.clinical_category: preeclampsia with severe features / hepatic laboratory abnormality
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current ACOG public guidance. The exact greater-than-twice-upper-limit liver-enzyme criterion and alternative-diagnosis qualifier are explicit, and the ACOG patient guidance independently identifies abnormal liver function as a severe feature.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: The stem reproduces the source-supported laboratory threshold and exclusion qualifier. A gives the correct clinical interpretation. B overcalls HELLP from one component. C falsely normalizes a qualifying end-organ abnormality. D assigns a hepatic marker to the wrong organ system.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; impaired hepatic function at this source-supported threshold is a severe feature.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect but plausible; elevated liver enzymes are part of HELLP, but HELLP cannot be established without the other syndrome components.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; the specified abnormality is clinically significant in preeclampsia rather than expected physiology.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; renal insufficiency is assessed with renal measures, not transaminase elevation.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The alternative-diagnosis exclusion in the stem prevents overattributing nonspecific transaminase abnormalities. Only A matches ACOG's severe-feature interpretation.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are interpretations of the same laboratory abnormality and are similar in specificity; no option is made correct by an emergency label or wording asymmetry.
audit_findings.blueprint: The construct is interpretation of a laboratory change signaling maternal complication, directly aligned with Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the exact ACOG threshold, the alternative-diagnosis caveat, HELLP overlap, and whether isolated transaminase elevation can be used as a severe feature.
